proposals.before: Prince Daizong of Jiangxia sought Jie's help in a matter; Jie reported it to the throne, and Emperor Taizong was pleased. He bestowed two hundred bolts of silk and comforted him, saying, "Of late I have not appointed left and right vice directors precisely because you are still in office."
proposals.after: Prince Daozong of Jiangxia sought Jie's help in a matter; Jie reported it to the throne, and Emperor Taizong was pleased. He bestowed two hundred bolts of silk and comforted him, saying, "Of late I have not appointed left and right vice directors precisely because you are still in office."
proposals.reason: Chinese 道宗 is Daozong, not Daizong; the translation misreads the personal name of the Prince of Jiangxia.

proposals.after: Prince Daozong of Jiangxia requested Jie's help in a matter; Jie reported it, and Emperor Taizong was pleased and bestowed two hundred bolts of silk, comforting him and saying: "Of late I have not appointed left and right vice directors because you are in the office."

proposals.before: Rong submitted reports on the selection process, but Shuo repeatedly turned them back. Enraged, Rong joined Vice Censor-in-Chief Cui Yinpu and others in a court impeachment, charging Shuo with employing shamans for ritual prayer and taking bribes. Shuo was stripped of the chancellorship.
proposals.after: Rong submitted reports on the selection process, but Shuo repeatedly turned them back. Enraged, Rong joined Censor-in-Chief Cui Yinpu and others in a court impeachment, charging Shuo with employing shamans for ritual prayer and taking bribes. Shuo was stripped of the chancellorship.
proposals.reason: 御史大夫 is Censor-in-Chief; 御史中丞 is Vice Censor-in-Chief. The translation understates Cui Yinpu's office.

proposals.before: He then recommended Song Jing for Right Chancellor, Pei Yaojing for Vice Director of the Treasury, and Xu Xianxian for Vice Director of Works. People at the time praised his eye for talent.
proposals.after: He then recommended Song Jing for Right Chancellor, Pei Yaoqing for Vice Director of the Treasury, and Xu Jingxian for Vice Director of Works. People at the time praised his eye for talent.
proposals.reason: 裴耀卿 is Pei Yaoqing (not Yaojing); 許景先 is Xu Jingxian (not Xianxian).

proposals.before: He then recommended Song Jing as Right Chancellor, Pei Yaojing as Vice Director of the Treasury, and Xu Xianxian as Vice Director of Works; contemporaries admired his discernment in men.
proposals.after: He then recommended Song Jing as Right Chancellor, Pei Yaoqing as Vice Director of the Treasury, and Xu Jingxian as Vice Director of Works; contemporaries admired his discernment in men.
proposals.reason: Align literal name spellings with 裴耀卿/許景先.

proposals.before: His son Zhun served as vice director of the Court of the Imperial Stud and entertained at cockfighting within the palace. Li Linfu's son You was also a favorite, but Zhun was wildly arrogant and treated You with open contempt.
proposals.after: His son Zhun served as vice director of the Court of the Imperial Insignia and entertained at cockfighting within the palace. Li Linfu's son You was also a favorite, but Zhun was wildly arrogant and treated You with open contempt.
proposals.reason: Chinese 衛尉少卿 is the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Guards), not the Imperial Stud (太仆寺).

decisions.reason: The source explicitly gives the prince's personal name as 道宗, Daozong. Daizong is a different name and is unsupported here.
The literal field repeats the same misreading of 道宗; Daozong is required in both English fields.
御史大夫 is Censor-in-Chief. Vice Censor-in-Chief would translate 御史中丞, which the source does not use for Cui Yinpu.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 與御史大夫崔隱甫等廷劾

decisions.reason: The source names 裴耀卿 and 許景先, correctly read Pei Yaoqing and Xu Jingxian. The earlier English misread both given names.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 裴耀卿為戶部侍郎，許景先為工部侍郎

decisions.reason: The literal field contains the same two name errors and should follow the names directly attested by 裴耀卿 and 許景先.
衛尉少卿 is the junior chamberlain of the Court of the Imperial Insignia, concerned with palace security. The Court of the Imperial Stud is 太僕寺 and is not named here.
